claim: DNA replication initiates from approximately 50,000 origins on human chromosomes in each cell cycle based on experimentally determined average inter-origin distances of ~100 kb.
source: Based on experimentally determined average inter-origin distances of ~100 kb, DNA replication initiates from ~50,000 origins on human chromosomes in each cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about inter-origin distances and inference about the number of origins.

claim: Out of ~7.5 million union origins identified by all datasets, only 0.27% (20,250 shared origins) were reproducibly obtained in at least 20 independent SNS-seq datasets and contained in initiation zones identified by each of three other techniques.
source: Out of ~7.5 million union origins identified by all datasets, only 0.27% (20,250 shared origins) were reproducibly obtained in at least 20 independent SNS-seq datasets and contained in initiation zones identified by each of three other techniques, suggesting extensive variability in origin usage and identification.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis of 113 genome-wide datasets presented in the manuscript.

claim: 21% of the shared origins overlap with transcriptional promoters.
source: Also, 21% of the shared origins overlap with transcriptional promoters, posing a conundrum.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only 6.4% of the 20,250 shared origins were within 1 kb from any of the ~13,000 reproducible ORC-binding sites in human cancer cells.
source: Only 6.4% of the 20,250 shared origins were within 1 kb from any of the ~13,000 reproducible ORC-binding sites in human cancer cells, and only 4.5% were within 1 kb of the ~11,000 union MCM2-7-binding sites in contrast to the nearly 100% overlap in the two comparisons in the yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis comparing human and yeast origins with ORC-binding sites.

claim: Only 4.5% of the 20,250 shared origins were within 1 kb of the ~11,000 union MCM2-7-binding sites.
source: Only 6.4% of the 20,250 shared origins were within 1 kb from any of the ~13,000 reproducible ORC-binding sites in human cancer cells, and only 4.5% were within 1 kb of the ~11,000 union MCM2-7-binding sites in contrast to the nearly 100% overlap in the two comparisons in the yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of MCM-binding sites and origins.

claim: Nearly 100% of yeast origins overlap with ORC-binding sites and MCM-binding sites.
source: Only 6.4% of the 20,250 shared origins were within 1 kb from any of the ~13,000 reproducible ORC-binding sites in human cancer cells, and only 4.5% were within 1 kb of the ~11,000 union MCM2-7-binding sites in contrast to the nearly 100% overlap in the two comparisons in the yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of yeast origins and binding sites.

claim: Human and most eukaryotic origins do not seem to have a clear DNA sequence preference.
source: Unlike yeast origins, human and most eukaryotic origins do not seem to have a clear DNA sequence preference (Hu and Stillman, 2023; Leonard and Méchali, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chromatin context and other DNA-based activity are important factors for human and non-yeast eukaryotic origin selection.
source: Yet it becomes clear that chromatin context and other DNA-based activity are important factors for human and non-yeast eukaryotic origin selection.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: G-quadruplex motifs were found to be associated with human origins.
source: For example, G-quadruplex motifs were found to be associated with human origins (Besnard et al., 2012), but can only explain a small subset of origins even after controlling for technical biases (Foulk et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: G-quadruplex motifs can only explain a small subset of origins even after controlling for technical biases.
source: For example, G-quadruplex motifs were found to be associated with human origins (Besnard et al., 2012), but can only explain a small subset of origins even after controlling for technical biases (Foulk et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: SNS-seq utilizes lambda exonuclease (λ-exo) to enrich RNA-primed newly replicated DNA by removing parental DNA fragments.
source: For instance, SNS-seq utilizes lambda exonuclease (λ-exo) to enrich RNA-primed newly replicated DNA by removing parental DNA fragments.
evidence: This claim describes the technical methodology of SNS-seq based on established knowledge.

claim: SNS-seq products may be contaminated with chromosomal DNA fragments or be affected by the cutting bias of λ-exo against guanine-cytosine (GC)-rich sequences.
source: However, the products may be contaminated with chromosomal DNA fragments or be affected by the cutting bias of λ-exo against guanine-cytosine (GC)-rich sequences (Foulk et al., 2015), although it has been proposed that one can experimentally correct and control for such biases (Akerman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research describing technical biases.

claim: SNS-seq is the only method that yields origins at a resolution of a few hundred base pairs, with all other methods delineating larger initiation zones (IZs) that may have multiple origins.
source: SNS-seq is the only method that yields origins at a resolution of a few hundred base pairs, with all other methods delineating larger initiation zones (IZs) that may have multiple origins.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of different sequencing techniques and their resolutions.

claim: Repli-seq results may be contaminated by DNA non-specifically associated with the antibody.
source: Repli-seq relies on nucleotide pulse labeling and antibody enrichment of newly replicated DNA superimposed on cells fractionated at different parts of the S phase by flow cytometry. Here the results may be contaminated by DNA non-specifically associated with the antibody (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research describing technical limitations.

claim: Rerep-seq origins tend to be enriched in the early replicating, epigenetically open parts of the genome.
source: Rerep-seq only captures the new synthesized sequences that replicate more than once when replication is dysregulated, and these origins tend to be enriched in the early replicating, epigenetically open parts of the genome (Menzel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and knowledge about Rerep-seq methodology.

claim: Bubble-seq generates long reads because it captures the origin-containing replication intermediates by selection of DNA bubbles, and so may enrich origins that are flanked by pause sites.
source: Bubble-seq (Mesner et al., 2013) generates long reads because it captures the origin-containing replication intermediates by selection of DNA bubbles, and so may enrich origins that are flanked by pause sites.
evidence: This claim is based on citation and inference about the technical characteristics of Bubble-seq.

claim: OK-seq identifies sites where the direction of the Okazaki fragments changes from leftward to rightward on the chromosome-revealing sites where the two lagging strands diverge from each other.
source: Okazaki-seq (OK-seq) identifies sites where the direction of the Okazaki fragments changes from leftward to rightward on the chromosome-revealing sites where the two lagging strands diverge from each other (Petryk et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation describing the OK-seq methodology.

claim: Yeast origin recognition complex (ORC) binds to double-stranded DNA with sequence specificity.
source: Yeast origin recognition complex (ORC) binds to double-stranded DNA with sequence specificity, helps load minichromosome maintenance protein complex (MCM), and thus prepares the origins for subsequent firing (Bell and Dutta, 2002; Remus et al., 2009; Bell and Stillman, 1992; Costa and Diffley, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Yeast ORC helps load minichromosome maintenance protein complex (MCM) and thus prepares the origins for subsequent firing.
source: Yeast origin recognition complex (ORC) binds to double-stranded DNA with sequence specificity, helps load minichromosome maintenance protein complex (MCM), and thus prepares the origins for subsequent firing (Bell and Dutta, 2002; Remus et al., 2009; Bell and Stillman, 1992; Costa and Diffley, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The role of ORC in loading MCM proteins was described in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Consistent with this, the role of ORC in loading MCM proteins was also described in Xenopus egg extracts (Rowles et al., 1999; Coleman et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human ORC shows very little sequence specificity in binding to double-stranded DNA sequences.
source: Efforts to define double-stranded DNA sequences bound specifically by human ORC find very little sequence specificity (Vashee et al., 2003; Hoshina et al., 2013), and this may be responsible for the lack of sequence specificity in human origins.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The difference between yeast and human ORC sequence specificity is attributed to sequence features in ORC4.
source: This difference between yeast and human ORC is attributed to sequence features in ORC4, one of the subunits of the ORC (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: When a yeast-specific 19 amino acid insert was removed from yeast ORC4 to make it more like the human ORC4, the sequence specificity of ORC binding was lost even in yeast.
source: When a yeast-specific 19 amino acid insert was removed from yeast ORC4 to make it more like the human ORC4, the sequence specificity of ORC binding was lost even in yeast.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited research about ORC4 mutations.

claim: Despite loss of sequence specificity, the mutant yeast ORC loaded MCM proteins, and the yeast replicated DNA and survived.
source: Despite this loss of sequence specificity, the mutant yeast ORC loaded MCM proteins, and the yeast replicated DNA and survived.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited research about mutant yeast ORC.

claim: Active origins and dormant origins determined by SNS-seq and OK-seq have little difference in ORC or MCM density.
source: An additional complexity is that genome-wide analysis found active origins and dormant origins determined by SNS-seq and OK-seq have little difference in ORC or MCM density (Sugimoto et al., 2018; Kirstein et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Significant MCM2-7 loading and DNA synthesis occur after genetic mutation of Drosophila ORC1 and human ORC1, ORC2, or ORC5 genes that reduce the expressed proteins to near undetectable levels.
source: Finally, a few publications have reported significant MCM2-7 loading and DNA synthesis after genetic mutation of Drosophila ORC1 and human ORC1, ORC2, or ORC5 genes that reduce the expressed proteins to near undetectable levels (Park and Asano, 2008; Shibata et al., 2016; Okano-Uchida et al., 2018; Shibata and Dutta, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The ORC2 gene was essential for viability in the cancer cell lines mutated for ORC2 according to sgRNA screens.
source: It should be noted, however, that sgRNA screens revealed that the ORC2 gene was essential for viability in the cancer cell lines mutated for ORC2, suggesting that vanishingly small amounts of the ORC2 gene product are required for some processes essential for cell proliferation (Chou et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A total of 7,459,709 union origins were discovered from all techniques.
source: A total of ~7,460,000 union origins were discovered from all techniques (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) of all origin datasets shows that origin profiles from the same technique are more similar to each other than from different techniques.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of all origin datasets shows that origin profiles from the same technique are more similar to each other than from different techniques (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Each method identifies origins that are best correlated with origins identified by that method alone.
source: This is confirmed by pairwise correlations of the datasets, where it is evident that each method identifies origins that are best correlated with origins identified by that method alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by pairwise correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rerep-seq and Bubble-seq seem to identify IZs that are also better correlated with SNS-seq origins.
source: Rerep-seq and Bubble-seq seem to identify IZs that are also better correlated with SNS-seq origins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: No clear trends of clustering of origins identified in similar cell types were observed.
source: However, we did not observe clear trends of clustering of origins identified in similar cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), even when we focused only on SNS-seq origins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and 1d.

claim: SNS-seq origins from T lymphoblasts were very closely clustered with each other in six datasets, but these were all done in the CCRF-CEM cell line (or a derivative) by one group at the same time.
source: The one exception was the SNS-seq origins from T lymphoblasts, which were very closely clustered with each other in six datasets, but these were all done in the CCRF-CEM cell line (or a derivative) by one group at the same time (Murai et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis and citation to the source of the datasets.

claim: SNS-seq datasets do not become progressively more reproducible as one goes year-by-year from 2018 to 2022.
source: However, SNS-seq datasets do not become progressively more reproducible as one goes year-by-year from 2018 to 2022 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Around half of the detected origins fall in intergenic regions, followed by 30–40% allocated to introns.
source: Regardless of the technique used, around half of the detected origins fall in intergenic regions, followed by 30–40% allocated to introns (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Origins in general have lower overlap with TF-binding hotspot (<0.5%) compared to the 16% overlap of gene promoter regions (transcription start sites [TSS]± 100bp) with such TF-binding hotspots.
source: Despite the differences among techniques, the origins in general have lower overlap with TF-binding hotspot (<0.5%) compared to the 16% overlap of gene promoter regions (transcription start sites [TSS]± 100bp) with such TF-binding hotspots (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Origins show significantly lower overlap with constitutive CTCF sites compared to promoters.
source: Origins show significantly lower overlap with constitutive CTCF sites, defined as those that are conserved across cell types (Fang et al., 2020), compared to promoters (Figure 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 1f and citation to the definition of constitutive CTCF sites.

claim: Origins defined by these techniques show significantly lower GC content compared to promoters.
source: However, compared to promoters, origins defined by these techniques show significantly lower GC content (Figure 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by GC content analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: There is a significantly lower overlap of these origins with G-quadruplex sites compared to the overlap of promoters with G-quadruplex sites.
source: In addition, there is a significantly lower overlap of these origins with G-quadruplex sites identified from the predicted G-quadruplex motif regions (Bedrat et al., 2016) compared to the overlap of promoters with G-quadruplex sites (Figure 1h).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 1h and citation to G-quadruplex prediction method.

claim: All origins, regardless of the technique by which they are identified, are slightly enriched at gene promoters, exons, or introns compared with the genome background.
source: We found that all origins, regardless of the technique by which they are identified, are slightly enriched at gene promoters, exons, or introns compared with the genome background (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Origins defined by Rerep-seq show the highest level of enrichment with promoters, TF hotspots, constitutive CTCF-binding sites and G-quadruplexes, and the highest GC content.
source: Among the five different techniques, origins defined by Rerep-seq show the highest level of enrichment with promoters, TF hotspots, constitutive CTCF-binding sites and G-quadruplexes, and the highest GC content.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of different techniques shown in the figures.

claim: Areas of the genome that are re-replicated when the cell cycle is disturbed are enriched in parts of the genome that replicate early in the S phase, regions that are enriched in transcriptionally active genes and their promoters.
source: This is consistent with our knowledge that areas of the genome that are re-replicated when the cell cycle is disturbed are enriched in parts of the genome that replicate early in the S phase, regions that are enriched in transcriptionally active (and thus epigenetically open) genes and their promoters.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about re-replication and early replicating regions.

claim: The shared origins have a greater overlap rate with gene promoters and exons compared to union origins.
source: The shared origins have a greater overlap rate with gene promoters and exons compared to union origins (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Replication and transcription are highly coordinated and enrichment of origins at TSS has been previously observed.
source: This is in line with the previous observation that replication and transcription are highly coordinated and enrichment of origins at TSS (Ganier et al., 2019; Cook, 1999; Karnani et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Shared origins have a substantially higher overlap rate than union origins with TF-binding hotspots.
source: Shared origins also have a substantially higher overlap rate than union origins with TF-binding hotspots (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Shared origins have a higher overlap rate with constitutive CTCF-binding sites compared to union origins.
source: Moreover, shared origins have a higher overlap rate with constitutive CTCF-binding sites compared to union origins (Figure 2e) and have a higher GC content and overlap with G-quadruplexes than union origins (Figure 2f and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Shared origins have a higher GC content and overlap with G-quadruplexes than union origins.
source: Moreover, shared origins have a higher overlap rate with constitutive CTCF-binding sites compared to union origins (Figure 2e) and have a higher GC content and overlap with G-quadruplexes than union origins (Figure 2f and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by GC content and G-quadruplex overlap analysis shown in Figure 2f and g.

claim: BART analysis identified potential TFs or components of chromatin remodeling factors (e.g., PAF1, EZH2, ZNF282, POLR2A, GTF2I) whose binding sites are associated with the shared origins.
source: We used BART to perform TF-binding site enrichment analysis on the shared origins and union origins and identified potential TFs or components of chromatin remodeling factors (e.g., PAF1, EZH2, ZNF282, POLR2A, GTF2I) whose binding sites are associated with the shared origins (Figure 2h, Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by BART analysis shown in Figure 2h.

claim: A substantial enrichment of activating histone marks, including H3K4me3 and H3/H4 acetylation, was observed at shared origins compared to union origins.
source: A substantial enrichment of activating histone marks, including H3K4me3 and H3/H4 acetylation, was observed at shared origins compared to union origins (Figure 2i).
evidence: This claim is supported by histone modification enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2i.

claim: H3K27me3, a repressive mark, is also enriched at shared origins, although this enrichment is not as high as that of the activating marks.
source: H3K27me3, a repressive mark, is also enriched at shared origins, although this enrichment is not as high as that of the activating marks.
evidence: This claim is supported by histone modification enrichment analysis.

claim: Among the 20,250 high-confidence shared origins, 9901 (48.9%) overlapped with SNS-seq origins in K562.
source: Among the 20,250 high-confidence shared origins, 9901 (48.9%) overlapped with SNS-seq origins in K562, 3872 (19.1%) overlapped with OK-seq IZs in K562, and 1163 (5.7%) overlapped with Repli-seq origins in K562.
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis of K562 cell line data.

claim: 3872 (19.1%) of the shared origins overlapped with OK-seq IZs in K562.
source: Among the 20,250 high-confidence shared origins, 9901 (48.9%) overlapped with SNS-seq origins in K562, 3872 (19.1%) overlapped with OK-seq IZs in K562, and 1163 (5.7%) overlapped with Repli-seq origins in K562.
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis of K562 cell line data.

claim: 1163 (5.7%) of the shared origins overlapped with Repli-seq origins in K562.
source: Among the 20,250 high-confidence shared origins, 9901 (48.9%) overlapped with SNS-seq origins in K562, 3872 (19.1%) overlapped with OK-seq IZs in K562, and 1163 (5.7%) overlapped with Repli-seq origins in K562.
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis of K562 cell line data.

claim: 2.7% of SNS-seq origins, 17.2% of OK-seq IZs, and 7.7% of Repli-seq IZs overlapped with the 20,250 shared origins.
source: In the opposite direction, where we estimate what fraction of origins found by a given technique fall in a reproducible origin, the opposite result emerges: 2.7% of SNS-seq origins, 17.2% of OK-seq IZs, and 7.7% of Repli-seq IZs overlapped with the 20,250 shared origins (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A total of 34,894 ORC-binding sites were identified in the human genome.
source: We identified a total of 34,894 ORC-binding sites in the human genome (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of ORC ChIP-seq datasets.

claim: Union (all) of ORC-binding sites are enriched at promoters, TF hotspots, constitutive CTCF sites, GC content, and G-quadruplexes compared to randomized genome background.
source: Union (all) of ORC-binding sites are enriched at promoters, TF hotspots, constitutive CTCF sites, GC content, and G-quadruplexes compared to randomized genome background (Figure 3a–e), somewhat similar to what we observed for the shared origins (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3a-e.

claim: 12,712 ORC-binding sites were defined as shared ORC-binding sites as they occur in at least two ORC datasets.
source: Of the 34,894 ORC-binding sites in the human genome, 12,712 sites were defined as shared ORC-binding sites as they occur in at least two ORC datasets (occupancy score ≥ 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis defining shared ORC-binding sites.

claim: 1.7% of the shared origins overlapped with shared ORC-binding sites.
source: The overlap was surprisingly low: 1.7% of the shared origins overlapped with shared ORC-binding sites (Figure 3f, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Only 1300 (6.4%) of the shared origins were proximal (≤1 kb) to the shared ORC-binding sites.
source: Even when we relaxed the criteria to look at the shared origins that are proximal (≤1 kb) to the shared ORC-binding sites, only 1300 (6.4%) of the shared origins were proximal to the shared ORC-binding sites (Figure 3f; Supplementary file 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Only 1086 (3.11%) ORC-binding sites are proximal to (≤1 kb) a shared replication origin.
source: A histogram of the distance between any ORC-binding site (union) and the nearest shared origin showed that only 1086 (3.11%) ORC-binding sites are proximal to (≤1 kb) a shared replication origin (Figure 3g, Supplementary file 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Only 8.8% of the 105,881 union origins identified by SNS-seq, OK-seq, or Repli-seq in K562 cells overlap with ORC2-binding sites mapped in the same cell line.
source: Only 8.8% of the 105,881 union origins identified by SNS-seq, OK-seq, or Repli-seq in K562 cells overlap with ORC2-binding sites mapped in the same cell line, and only 4.9% of the 68,003 union SNS-seq origins mapped in HeLa cells overlap with ORC1-binding sites in the same cell line.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell line-specific overlap analysis.

claim: Only 4.9% of the 68,003 union SNS-seq origins mapped in HeLa cells overlap with ORC1-binding sites in the same cell line.
source: Only 8.8% of the 105,881 union origins identified by SNS-seq, OK-seq, or Repli-seq in K562 cells overlap with ORC2-binding sites mapped in the same cell line, and only 4.9% of the 68,003 union SNS-seq origins mapped in HeLa cells overlap with ORC1-binding sites in the same cell line.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell line-specific overlap analysis.

claim: 12.8% of 9605 shared origins in K562 cells overlap with ORC2 ChIP-seq sites in the concordant cell line.
source: The overlaps improve marginally if we focus on the shared origins: 12.8% of 9605 shared origins in K562 cells and 6.1% of 3390 shared origins in HeLa cells overlap with ORC2 and ORC1 ChIP-seq sites in the concordant cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell line-specific overlap analysis of shared origins.

claim: 6.1% of 3390 shared origins in HeLa cells overlap with ORC1 ChIP-seq sites in the concordant cell line.
source: The overlaps improve marginally if we focus on the shared origins: 12.8% of 9605 shared origins in K562 cells and 6.1% of 3390 shared origins in HeLa cells overlap with ORC2 and ORC1 ChIP-seq sites in the concordant cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell line-specific overlap analysis of shared origins.

claim: In yeast S. cerevisiae, 100% of the shared origins are proximate to (≤1 kb) all (union) or shared ORC-binding sites.
source: In this case, 100% of the shared origins are proximate to (≤1 kb) all (union) or shared ORC-binding sites in yeast (Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast data analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: 1300 shared origins are proximate to a shared ORC-binding site, representing the 'highest-confidence origins'.
source: Because of the poor co-localization of shared origins with ORC-binding sites, we next focused on 6.4% of shared origins (1300) that are proximate to a shared ORC-binding site, a group we will call the 'highest-confidence origins'.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis defining a subset of origins.

claim: The 1300 'highest confidence origins' are even more co-localized with gene promoters compared with the shared origins or ORC-binding sites alone.
source: Compared with the shared origins or ORC-binding sites alone, these 1300 origins are even more co-localized with gene promoters (Figure 4a), TF-binding hotspots (Figure 4b), and constitutive CTCF-binding sites (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The 'highest confidence origins' are even more co-localized with TF-binding hotspots compared with the shared origins or ORC-binding sites alone.
source: Compared with the shared origins or ORC-binding sites alone, these 1300 origins are even more co-localized with gene promoters (Figure 4a), TF-binding hotspots (Figure 4b), and constitutive CTCF-binding sites (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The 'highest confidence origins' are even more co-localized with constitutive CTCF-binding sites compared with the shared origins or ORC-binding sites alone.
source: Compared with the shared origins or ORC-binding sites alone, these 1300 origins are even more co-localized with gene promoters (Figure 4a), TF-binding hotspots (Figure 4b), and constitutive CTCF-binding sites (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The GC content is not significantly higher for the 'highest confidence origins'.
source: The GC content is not significantly higher for these 'highest confidence origins' (Figure 4d), and neither was their overlap with G-quadruplexes (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is supported by GC content analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The overlap with G-quadruplexes is not significantly higher for the 'highest confidence origins'.
source: The GC content is not significantly higher for these 'highest confidence origins' (Figure 4d), and neither was their overlap with G-quadruplexes (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is supported by G-quadruplex overlap analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The mean replication timing score of shared origins suggests that they replicate earlier in the S phase compared to the union origins.
source: To understand the correlation between the different classes of origins and replication timing, we calculated the replication timing score for the origins following the ENCODE pipeline (Navarro Gonzalez et al., 2021; Hansen et al., 2010) and found that the mean replication timing score of shared origins suggests that they replicate earlier in the S phase compared to the union origins, but there is not much difference between the shared origins separated by whether they overlapped with the ORC-binding sites or not (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by replication timing analysis shown in Figure 4f and citations to the methodology.

claim: There is not much difference in replication timing between the shared origins separated by whether they overlapped with the ORC-binding sites or not.
source: To understand the correlation between the different classes of origins and replication timing, we calculated the replication timing score for the origins following the ENCODE pipeline (Navarro Gonzalez et al., 2021; Hansen et al., 2010) and found that the mean replication timing score of shared origins suggests that they replicate earlier in the S phase compared to the union origins, but there is not much difference between the shared origins separated by whether they overlapped with the ORC-binding sites or not (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by replication timing analysis shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The genes co-localized with the highest confidence origins exhibit higher expression levels compared to the genes co-localized with all shared origins or union origins.
source: To investigate whether the 'highest confidence origins' (shared origins near the ORC-binding sites) are associated with higher transcriptional activity, we divided all human genes into four groups based on their expression level in the human K562 cell line and found that the genes co-localized with the highest confidence origins exhibit higher expression levels compared to the genes co-localized with all shared origins or union origins (Figure 4g).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4g.

claim: BART analysis of 743 origins overlapping with any ORC-binding sites shows that the ORC2-binding sites are enriched near these origins.
source: BART analysis (Wang et al., 2018) of which protein-binding sites are most enriched in 743 origins overlapping with any ORC-binding sites shows, as expected, that the ORC2-binding sites are enriched near these origins.
evidence: This claim is supported by BART analysis and citation to the methodology.

claim: The other proteins bound near the 743 origins overlapping with ORC-binding sites are either transcriptional activators like EPC1, LEF1, ELK, EGR1, PAF1, or transcriptional repressors like KLF13, KRAB, ZNF639, or ZBTB33.
source: The other proteins bound near these origins are either transcriptional activators like EPC1, LEF1, ELK, EGR1, PAF1, or transcriptional repressors like KLF13, KRAB, ZNF639, or ZBTB33 (Figure 4h).
evidence: This claim is supported by BART analysis shown in Figure 4h.

claim: A total of 11,394 MCM3-7-binding sites (union) were identified.
source: We identified a total of 11,394 MCM3-7-binding sites (union) and 3209 shared MCM-binding sites that are defined by an intersection of MCM3, MCM5, and MCM7 union peaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of MCM ChIP-seq datasets.

claim: 3209 shared MCM-binding sites were identified that are defined by an intersection of MCM3, MCM5, and MCM7 union peaks.
source: We identified a total of 11,394 MCM3-7-binding sites (union) and 3209 shared MCM-binding sites that are defined by an intersection of MCM3, MCM5, and MCM7 union peaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of MCM ChIP-seq datasets.

claim: MCM-binding sites displayed very similar genomic features to the ORC-binding sites.
source: Overall, MCM-binding sites displayed very similar genomic features to the ORC-binding sites (Figure 5a–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative genomic feature analysis shown in Figure 5a-e.

claim: Around 95% of yeast origins are close to (≤1 kb) the union of all yeast MCM sites.
source: Very interestingly, similar to the high overlap between yeast origins and yeast ORC sites (Figure 3f), around 95% of yeast origins (Lee et al., 2021; Gros et al., 2015) are close to (≤1 kb) the union of all yeast MCM sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast data analysis and citations to prior research.

claim: Only ~4.5% of shared human origins are close to (≤1 kb) the union of experimentally defined human MCM-binding sites.
source: In contrast, only ~4.5% of shared human origins are close to (≤1 kb) the union of experimentally defined human MCM-binding sites (Figure 5g).
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Only 3.8% of union origins overlap with union MCM3-7-binding sites in K562 cells.
source: Even if we focus on the limited data from the same cell line (K562 or HCT116), only 3.8% (union origins) or 5.5% shared origins overlap with union MCM3-7-binding sites in K562 cells and 19.5% of union origins overlap with any MCM2-binding sites in HCT116 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, c, and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell line-specific overlap analysis.

claim: 5.5% of shared origins overlap with union MCM3-7-binding sites in K562 cells.
source: Even if we focus on the limited data from the same cell line (K562 or HCT116), only 3.8% (union origins) or 5.5% shared origins overlap with union MCM3-7-binding sites in K562 cells and 19.5% of union origins overlap with any MCM2-binding sites in HCT116 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, c, and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell line-specific overlap analysis.

claim: 19.5% of union origins overlap with any MCM2-binding sites in HCT116 cells.
source: Even if we focus on the limited data from the same cell line (K562 or HCT116), only 3.8% (union origins) or 5.5% shared origins overlap with union MCM3-7-binding sites in K562 cells and 19.5% of union origins overlap with any MCM2-binding sites in HCT116 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, c, and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell line-specific overlap analysis.

claim: 22% of the shared origins are proximate to the phospho-S108 MCM2-binding sites.
source: Phospho-S108 MCM2 showed the best result among the phospho-isoforms tested, with 22% of the shared origins being proximate to the phospho-S108 MCM2-binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity analysis of phosphorylated MCM2 isoforms.

claim: Only 1363 (21%) of the 6501 ORC1 peaks overlapped with the 29,930 ORC2 peaks.
source: Only 1363 (21%) of the 6501 ORC1 peaks overlapped with the 29,930 ORC2 peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), and the vast majority (68%) of ORC1 peaks are far away (≥2 kb) from the closest ORC2 peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The vast majority (68%) of ORC1 peaks are far away (≥2 kb) from the closest ORC2 peaks.
source: Only 1363 (21%) of the 6501 ORC1 peaks overlapped with the 29,930 ORC2 peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), and the vast majority (68%) of ORC1 peaks are far away (≥2 kb) from the closest ORC2 peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: 74 origins were reproducibly identified by multiple methods (shared origins near ORC-binding sites, MCM3-7-binding sites, and MCM2-binding sites).
source: We examined all three types of high-confidence origins (ORC designated, MCM3-7 designated and MCM2 designated) in a Venn diagram (Figure 5h) and identified 74 that were reproducibly identified by multiple methods (shared origins near ORC-binding sites, MCM3-7-binding sites, and MCM2-binding sites).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 5h.

claim: The shared (highly reproducible) origins are only a small subset of all origins identified and are in epigenetically active chromatin with a strong preference for promoters.
source: The following conclusions were reached: the shared (highly reproducible) origins are only a small subset of all origins identified and are in epigenetically active chromatin with a strong preference for promoters.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: G-quadruplexes, CTCF-binding sites, and ORC-binding sites are enriched near the promoters, so although these genomic features are enriched near the shared origins, it is not clear whether these genomic features actually specify origins or whether they are simply enriched near origins because the origins are near the promoters.
source: However, G-quadruplexes, CTCF-binding sites, and ORC-binding sites are also enriched near the promoters, so although these genomic features are enriched near the shared origins, it is not clear whether these genomic features actually specify origins or whether they are simply enriched near origins because the origins are near the promoters.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference from the data analysis.

claim: The co-localization of the shared origins with ORC- or MCM2-7- binding sites is very low, much lower than that in yeast.
source: Finally, our results suggest that the co-localization of the shared origins with ORC- or MCM2-7- binding sites is very low, much lower than that in yeast, and so (a) the currently known binding sites of these proteins should not be used as surrogate markers of origins in human cells and (b) there is a great need to improve our methods of identifying isoforms of these proteins that are strictly functional for origin firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparative data analysis between human and yeast.

claim: The currently known binding sites of ORC and MCM proteins should not be used as surrogate markers of origins in human cells.
source: Finally, our results suggest that the co-localization of the shared origins with ORC- or MCM2-7- binding sites is very low, much lower than that in yeast, and so (a) the currently known binding sites of these proteins should not be used as surrogate markers of origins in human cells and (b) there is a great need to improve our methods of identifying isoforms of these proteins that are strictly functional for origin firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference from the low co-localization data.

claim: There is a great need to improve our methods of identifying isoforms of ORC and MCM proteins that are strictly functional for origin firing.
source: Finally, our results suggest that the co-localization of the shared origins with ORC- or MCM2-7- binding sites is very low, much lower than that in yeast, and so (a) the currently known binding sites of these proteins should not be used as surrogate markers of origins in human cells and (b) there is a great need to improve our methods of identifying isoforms of these proteins that are strictly functional for origin firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference from the data limitations.

claim: Individual methods produce origin datasets that are more correlated with each other than across methods.
source: A careful analysis shows that individual methods produce origin datasets that are more correlated with each other than across methods.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of the datasets.

claim: The extensive variation of origins between datasets is likely because of background noise in all current techniques and because there is extreme stochasticity of origin selection during DNA replication in individual cells and cell cycles in the same population of cells from a human cell line in culture.
source: The extensive variation of origins between datasets is likely because of background noise in all current techniques and because there is extreme stochasticity of origin selection during DNA replication in individual cells and cell cycles in the same population of cells from a human cell line in culture.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variation in the data.

claim: H3K4me3 has been reported to be enriched at replication origins.
source: H3K4me3 has been reported to be enriched at replication origins (Picard et al., 2014; Cayrou et al., 2015), and it has also been reported that demethylation of H3K4me3 by KDM5C/JARID1C promotes origin active (Rondinelli et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Demethylation of H3K4me3 by KDM5C/JARID1C promotes origin activity.
source: H3K4me3 has been reported to be enriched at replication origins (Picard et al., 2014; Cayrou et al., 2015), and it has also been reported that demethylation of H3K4me3 by KDM5C/JARID1C promotes origin active (Rondinelli et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: H3ac/H4ac are reported to be enriched at replication origins.
source: H3ac/H4ac are also reported to be enriched at replication origins (Cadoret et al., 2008; Sequeira-Mendes et al., 2009), and this is regulated by various histone acetyltransferases and histone deacetylases (Goren et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: H3K27me3 has been reported to be enriched at replication origins.
source: Interestingly, H3K27me3 has also been reported to be enriched at replication origins (Picard et al., 2014; Cayrou et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: H3K9me3 has been reported to be enriched near late replicating origins.
source: H3K9me3 has been reported to be enriched near late replicating origins (Wang et al., 2017), while the shared origins are biased toward those that are in euchromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The overlap of shared origins with promoters (TSS ±4 kb), G-quadruplexes, R-loops, and CTCF-binding sites are all significantly above the background.
source: The overlap of shared origins with promoters (TSS ±4 kb), G-quadruplexes, R-loops, and CTCF-binding sites are all significantly above the background.
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The overlap of promoters with G-quadruplexes, R loops, and CTCF-binding sites are also all significantly above the background.
source: However, the overlap of promoters with G-quadruplexes, R loops, and CTCF-binding sites are also all significantly above the background, though the enrichment of G-quadruplexes is minimal.
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: G-quadruplexes have been experimentally shown to dictate origin specification.
source: G-quadruplexes are of particular interest because they have been experimentally shown to dictate origin specification (Prorok et al., 2019; Valton et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental research.

claim: The overlap of shared origins with G-quadruplexes is 3.5-fold above random while that of promoters with G-quadruplexes is only 1.3-fold above random.
source: However, the overlap of shared origins with G-quadruplexes is 3.5-fold above random while that of promoters with G-quadruplexes is only 1.3-fold above random, which would be consistent with the idea that G-quadruplexes have a role in specifying origins and the overlap is not simply due to the proximity of origins with promoters.
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test analysis and inference about the role of G-quadruplexes.

claim: CTCF-binding sites have been proposed to contribute to origin specification.
source: Similarly, CTCF-binding sites have been proposed to contribute to origin specification (Emerson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The enrichment of origins near the CTCF-binding sites (4.3-fold above random background) is comparable to the enrichment of promoters near the same sites (4.5-fold).
source: Here, though, the permutation test in Table 2 reveals that the enrichment of origins near the CTCF-binding sites (4.3-fold above random background) is comparable to the enrichment of promoters near the same sites (4.5-fold).
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: MCM2-7 are either loaded far from the ORC-binding sites or move significant distances after loading in the Xenopus egg extracts.
source: There is significant evidence for possibility (b). MCM2-7 are either loaded far from the ORC-binding sites or move significant distances after loading in the Xenopus egg extracts (Harvey and Newport, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In yeasts, there is evidence that MCM2-7 are pushed far away from the bodies of transcriptionally active genes by the RNA polymerase II and initiate replication at sites distant from where they are loaded on chromatin by ORC.
source: In yeasts, there is evidence that MCM2-7 are pushed far away from the bodies of transcriptionally active genes by the RNA polymerase II and initiate replication at sites distant from where they are loaded on chromatin by ORC (Gros et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In Drosophila, cyclin E/cdk2 kinase activity promotes the loading of a vast excess of MCM2-7 on chromatin relative to ORC, and the MCM2-7 complexes move away from their loading sites due to the activity of the transcriptional apparatus.
source: Similar observations have been made in Drosophila, where cyclin E/cdk2 kinase activity promotes the loading of a vast excess of MCM2-7 on chromatin relative to ORC, and the MCM2-7 complexes move away from their loading sites due to the activity of the transcriptional apparatus (Powell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: ORC1 has been reported to bind to RNA near promoters and stimulate replication from such sites.
source: ORC1 has also been reported to bind to RNA near promoters and stimulate replication from such sites (Mas et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The co-localization of TSS with ORC is more than the co-localization of shared origins with ORC according to random permutation test.
source: Thus, our observation that ORC is highly enriched near promoters is expected, the main advance being that the random permutation test suggests that co-localization of TSS with ORC is more than the co-localization of shared origins with ORC.
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation test analysis.

claim: A substantial fraction of ORC2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 bind to chromatin in the absence of ORC1.
source: We prefer the latter explanation because of our experimental result that a substantial fraction of ORC2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 bind to chromatin in the absence of ORC1, and ORC2, 3, and 6 bind to chromatin normally in the absence of ORC5 (Park and Asano, 2008; Shibata et al., 2016; Okano-Uchida et al., 2018; Shibata and Dutta, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental research.

claim: ORC2, 3, and 6 bind to chromatin normally in the absence of ORC5.
source: We prefer the latter explanation because of our experimental result that a substantial fraction of ORC2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 bind to chromatin in the absence of ORC1, and ORC2, 3, and 6 bind to chromatin normally in the absence of ORC5 (Park and Asano, 2008; Shibata et al., 2016; Okano-Uchida et al., 2018; Shibata and Dutta, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental research.

claim: Human ORC2, 3, 4, and 5 form a stable subcomplex, with much looser association of the subcomplex with ORC1 and ORC6.
source: We and others have also noted that human ORC2, 3, 4, and 5 form a stable subcomplex, with much looser association of the subcomplex with ORC1 and ORC6 (Dhar et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The 74 experimentally reproduced origin datasets with proximity to ORC and MCM2-7 ChIP-seq sites provide a starting list for experimental queries about whether genomic features independently specify the origins of replication and promoters of transcription.
source: Thus, although the overlaps are statistically significant, this correlation analysis cannot determine whether the same genomic features independently specify the origins of replication and promoters of transcription. This is a question that should be asked experimentally, and the 74 experimentally reproduced origin datasets with proximity to ORC and MCM2-7 ChIP-seq sites provide a starting list for such experimental queries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference about future experimental directions.
